role: Hardware monitoring for CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, memory, I/O and network silicon on Linux, Windows and macOS, with an entity ontology an agent reads before it queries anything: every value the tool can report, with its unit and its provenance. Reports what it cannot read as well as what it can, so an absent reading is a stated gap rather than a zero.

capabilities.name: monitor.describe
capabilities.description: Print the entity ontology: every value this can report, with its unit and provenance. Pure — touches no hardware, so the answer is identical on every machine and can be fetched before the machine is.

capabilities.name: monitor.get
capabilities.description: Read one ontology entity by id.

capabilities.name: monitor.snapshot
capabilities.description: Read every resolvable entity at once, with provenance for each, and name the ones that did not resolve.

capabilities.name: monitor.profile
capabilities.description: Inspect hardware profiles and tunable driver settings, and list which of them this build can write.

capabilities.name: monitor.profile_set
capabilities.description: Write a tunable driver or hardware setting. Refuses without --confirm, and refuses any id with no registered handler.

capabilities.name: monitor.tune
capabilities.description: Detect what the machine is being used for and recommend a hardware profile. Recommends; does not apply.

capabilities.name: monitor.record
capabilities.description: Record system metrics to a time-series database for later analysis.

capabilities.name: monitor.ids
capabilities.description: Intrusion detection over listening sockets and watched files.

capabilities.name: monitor.serve
capabilities.description: Serve the REST API and Prometheus metrics over HTTP.

capabilities.name: monitor.privacy
capabilities.description: Manage data-collection consent. IronMonitor collects and transmits nothing today, so a denial records a decision rather than stopping anything.

unmapped.why: This reports values with their units and provenance. Whether a temperature is too high for this machine, or a queue depth indicates a problem, is a judgement nothing here makes.

`tune` recommends a profile and does not apply one, and `profile set` writes only an id with a registered handler. Nothing here schedules, throttles, migrates or restarts anything; that is the host's business and IronWarden's.

Exactly one setting id has a registered write handler on this build. Every other setting the profile subsystem can read is read-only here, so an agent that finds a setting cannot assume it can change it — `profile writable` is the list that answers that, and it is short.

Readings come from what the OS and the vendor drivers expose. A subsystem with no driver, no permission or no sensor is reported as unresolved rather than as zero, which is the distinction this component is built around — but it means absence here is absence of access, not absence of hardware.

note: Written 2026-09-14, this component's first manifest, after it was renamed from Silicon Monitor and moved to ai/IronMonitor. Capabilities are the binary's own subcommands, read off `--help`; `gui`, `tui` and `cli` are surfaces rather than capabilities, because they are ways in rather than things done. `monitor.profile_set` was first declared `physical` here, on the reasoning that the subsystem is tunable driver settings in the style of XTU and Ryzen Master and those can damage equipment. IronStack refused it: a `physical` consequence from the `substrates` layer is a category error, because only `embodiment` actuates. That is the better argument and the declaration follows it. It is `data` instead, which is the nearest honest value rather than an exact one -- the only writable id on this build is `active_scheme_guid`, a Windows power scheme, and what it changes is persistent machine configuration, which the vocabulary has no class for. If a clock or voltage handler is ever registered, this declaration has to be revisited and the layer question with it. `requires_grant` is true for `profile_set` and for `serve`, which opens a port. Neither is budgeted, and that is deliberate rather than unconsidered: a budget meters a resource that runs out, and neither writing one setting nor binding one socket consumes anything a caller could exhaust. Everything else reads what the OS already exposes to the user running it.
